  entire [flags]
  entire [command]

  agent                      Manage agent integrations (add, remove, list)
  clean                      Clean up Entire session data
  configure                  Update Entire settings in the current repository
  disable                    Disable Entire in current repository
  doctor                     Diagnose and fix session issues

# Skill: but

# GitButler CLI Skill

Use GitButler CLI (`but`) as the default version-control interface.

## Start Here

Choose the narrowest first command by task; avoid ritual status checks:

```bash
# Selected dirty files/hunks:
but diff

# Commit order, branch/stack placement, conflict overview:
but status

# File IDs, per-commit files, amend details:
but status -fv

# What one applied branch or commit changed, for review:
but diff <branch-or-commit>

# Details for one known branch or commit:
but show <id>
```

Do not run plain `but status` and then `but status -fv` unless the compact output lacks file details needed for the task.

For "commit just/only/specific changes on a new branch", use the fast path:

```bash
but diff
but commit -b <branch> -m "<msg>" <id> <id>
```

`but commit -b <branch> ...` creates the branch when it does not exist and prints the created commit. Do not run a separate `but branch new`, status command, or verification diff unless the task needs workspace information that the result does not provide.

In a linked worktree, such as `.claude/worktrees/*`, omit `-b` so the commit goes on the branch the worktree has checked out. Use that branch as the new branch; do not stack another one on it. A worktree with a detached HEAD has no branch yet. There, `but commit -b <new-name> -m "<msg>"` creates the branch at HEAD, checks it out in that worktree, and commits to it.

## IDs

The first token on each `but diff` / `but status` line is that line's ID. When a command needs an ID, copy it exactly from the current output; never hardcode or invent one. ID lifetimes differ by entity:

- Changes and sources are **positional, space-separated** IDs (`but commit -b feat -m "msg" uvw:2e4 uvw:e2c`). An uncommitted hunk ID is written `<file-id>:<hunk-id>` (e.g. `uvw:2e4`, copied from bare `but diff`) — the part after the colon is the hunk's ID, **not** a line range (`uvw:16-40` is invalid). Do not invent flags like `--changes` / `--hunk` / `--ids`, pass a line range, or comma-separate IDs — `uvw,qyo` is parsed as one ID and fails.
- `but diff` is the exception: it accepts at most **one** target. Bare `but diff` shows all uncommitted files; inspect committed files or other entities one target at a time — never `but diff <id> <id>`.
- A committed file is `<commit-id>:<file-id>` (e.g. `mzm:uvw`, shown under each commit). A committed hunk is `<commit-id>:<file-id>:<hunk-id>` and is shown by `but diff <commit-id>`. `@` means the uncommitted area.
- Commit IDs are stable change IDs that survive history edits (`amend`, `squash`, `move`, `uncommit`, `reword`). Commits without a change ID (e.g. upstream-only) lead with a sha prefix instead, and `#N`-suffixed refs disambiguate duplicates — both go stale after history edits, and a stale sha can silently resolve to the wrong commit. The `(sha …)` on verbose commit lines is informational — do not pass it to commands.
- Branch short IDs are snapshot-local selectors. Use full branch names for branch-targeting mutations; short IDs are safe only for immediate read-only inspection.
- File/hunk IDs copied from one diff read generally remain usable across chained commits. If one stops resolving, re-read `but diff` and retry.

**Chaining:** mutation output is concise by default, so you may chain mutations with `&&` off one inspection read. Do not chain branch short IDs through mutations; use full branch names. Add `--status-after` only when the next step needs workspace IDs or details that the mutation result does not provide. Chained `but commit` calls stack in the order written — the first is oldest, each later one goes on top. History edits may run in sequence when every commit ref involved is a change-ID ref; run them one at a time with `--status-after` when a ref is sha-based or `#N`-suffixed, or when the next command needs freshly issued IDs. Chaining `but uncommit <id> && but diff` is safe because bare `diff` needs no ID from the uncommit output. Never pipe a mutation through `tail` or `head`: the pipeline then exits with their status, so the next `&&` runs even when the mutation failed.

## Non-Negotiable Rules

1. Use `but` for all write operations. Never run `git add`, `git commit`, `git push`, `git fetch`, `git pull`, `git checkout`, `git merge`, `git rebase`, `git stash`, or `git cherry-pick`; `but pull --check` fetches. The only exceptions are selecting a side of a conflicted submodule in resolution mode (see Resolve conflicted commits) and creating a missing target branch (see Notes). If the user says a `git` write command, translate it to `but` and run that.
2. Mutation commands print their result without appending workspace status. Add `--status-after` only when the next step needs resulting workspace IDs or details; otherwise trust the mutation result and do not run a verification status/diff.
3. Branches marked `(merged upstream)` have landed; start new work on another branch. That marker alone does not mean `but pull` removes them: run `but pull --check` first. `but pull` removes only branches listed `[integrated]` ("has been integrated upstream and removed locally", or "has been merged into <target> and removed" when the target has no upstream) and rebases the rest, which stay applied. To clear a landed branch that stays applied, use `but unapply <branch>` (acts on its whole stack) rather than `but discard`. `push` and mutations (`commit`, `amend`, `squash`, `uncommit`, `reword`, `move`) refuse landed branches and commits, `absorb` skips them with a notice, and `commit` skips them when picking a default target.
4. Keep going between routine `but` commands. Put any status note in the same message as the next command, and don't end a turn on a summary that announces the next `but` step without running it. Finish with a concise summary.
5. Prefer this skill and `but skill reference` over exploratory help calls. Use `<command> --help` when required syntax is missing or a command fails; use top-level help only when you genuinely need to discover an undocumented command.
6. Other agents may share this checkout, so `@` can hold their edits. Commit, amend, and discard only the IDs or paths you changed. Bare `but commit`, `but absorb`, `but discard @`, and `git stash` take their work too, and a refusal naming files you didn't edit means you selected theirs.

## Command Patterns

- Initialize a Git repository: `but init` (current directory) or `but -C <path> init`. Non-interactive; creates no commits, remotes, or GitButler workspace. Existing repositories are left unchanged. In a repository with no commits, make the first commit with a bare `but commit -m "<msg>"`; `-b` is refused there.

- Commit: `but commit -b <branch> -m "<msg>" <id> <id>` — `-b <branch>` creates the branch if it does not exist
- Commit everything uncommitted: `but commit -b <branch> -m "<msg>"` (omit the IDs)
- Several commits from one diff: chain `but commit` calls with `&&` (commits stack oldest-first)
- Never pass `-s` to `commit`, `move`, or `pick`: it is `--switch`, not git's `--signoff`, and it unapplies every other stack.
- The branch is never positional (`but commit <branch>` fails; use `-b`), `but amend` always needs `-t`, and `but diff` takes one target (use a shared `dir/` or one call each).
- Commit at a specific history position: `--above <commit-or-branch>` or `--below <commit-or-branch>` (mutually exclusive). With a branch target, add `-b <new-name>` to name the new branch; otherwise its name is generated. The name must not already exist. Do not combine `-b` (even without a name) with commit/worktree targets.
- Targeting is **required** when more than one **stack** is applied; without it `but commit` fails with "Unclear where to commit. Found more than one stack". Several branches stacked together count as one stack — an untargeted commit then silently lands on the stack's top branch, so pass `-b` whenever the branch matters.
- Always pass `-m "<msg>"` (or `-F -` with a heredoc, `-F <file>` with a file outside the repository, or `--no-message`) to `but commit`, and to `but squash` whenever its sources are commits or branches unless the target is `@` (squash also takes `-u` to keep the target's message) — those compose a new message; without a flag an agent run keeps whatever the command composed (empty for `but commit`, the joined source messages for `but squash`) and a terminal opens an editor. Squash sources that are uncommitted or committed changes reuse the target's message and need no flag; squashing into `@` rejects message flags outright.
- Amend: `but amend -t <commit-or-branch> <file-or-hunk-id> <file-or-hunk-id>` — a branch target resolves to its newest commit
- Uncommit: `but uncommit <commit-id>` (whole commit), `but uncommit <branch>` (all commits and remove branch), `but uncommit <commit-id>:<file-id>` (committed file), or `but uncommit <commit-id>:<file-id>:<hunk-id>` (committed hunk); committed files and hunks may be mixed, but all must come from one commit
- Copy commits (sources stay unchanged): `but pick <sha> [<sha>...] -b <new-branch>` puts the copies on a new independent branch from the target, `-b <existing-branch>` on that applied branch's tip, and `--above <branch> -b <new-name>` (or `--below`) on a new branch stacked there. Pick applies sources in the order given, so pass them oldest first. For a branch that is not applied, list SHAs with `git log --reverse <target>..<branch>` and inspect them with `git show` or `but show <sha>`; `but diff` and the IDs that `but branch show` prints for it do not work.
- Move committed changes into an existing commit or `@`: `but squash <commit-id>:<file-id> -t <commit-id-or-@>` for a committed file; `but squash <commit-id>:<file-id>:<hunk-id> -t <commit-id-or-@>` for a committed hunk; all sources must come from one commit
- Move committed changes into a new commit at a chosen position: `but move <commit-id>:<file-id> --above <commit-or-branch> -m "<msg>"` for a committed file; `but move <commit-id>:<file-id>:<hunk-id> --above <commit-or-branch> -m "<msg>"` for a committed hunk (`--below`, `--branch`, and `--unstack` also work)
- `but split` and a `but move` of committed changes name their new commit with `-m` or `-F` too; without either the commit gets an empty message. `but move` rejects `-m`/`-F` for whole-commit and branch sources.
- Move commit to branch top: `but move <commit-id> -b <branch>`
- Move commits or committed changes onto a new named branch: `but move <source> --above <branch> -b <new-name>` (`--below` also works); use `but move <source> --unstack -b <new-name>` for an independent branch. Omit `-b` for a generated name. Naming is not supported when stacking or unstacking a branch source.
- Discard: `but discard <id> [<id>...]` — accepts branches, commits, committed changes, uncommitted changes, or `@` for all uncommitted changes
- Push: `but push <top-branch>` — pushes the selected branch and its ancestors; to update a stack, select its top branch once and never loop. Bare `but push` pushes all unpushed work when run non-interactively — one push per stack (its topmost unpushed branch, ancestors included), and the output lists every branch it pushed. It exits non-zero if any stack failed; stacks that already pushed stay pushed, and rerunning after fixing the failure is safe (up-to-date stacks are skipped). `but push` and `but pr new` replace the remote branch: if others may have pushed to it, bring their commits in first (see Bring in commits pushed to a branch's own remote).
- Create PR: `but pr new <branch-name> [-m "Title..."] [-F - | -F <file>] [-t] [--draft]` — auto-pushes first; do not run `but push` before it

## Task Recipes

### Update workspace from main

For "get latest from main", "update/sync this workspace", "rebase onto main", or "pull main":

1. `but pull` — one command; no preflight needed. Its output reports the resulting state, and `but undo` reverts it. Uncommitted changes that conflict with the update get conflict markers and show as `{conflicted}`; resolve them as in Conflicts in uncommitted files.
2. If commits come back conflicted, resolve them with the `but resolve conflicts <branch>` and `but resolve apply` loop in Resolve conflicted commits, one branch at a time. When `HEAD` is `gitbutler/workspace`, `but pull` prints `but resolve <commit>` as the next step; that is edit mode, which is only for running code against a resolution.

`but pull --check` answers "would this conflict?" without updating. Do not use it as a routine
preflight; use it when the user asks for a preview, you need a fetch, repository policy requires one, other agents'
branches may move, or an applied branch was just merged upstream (see rule 3).

Rebasing applied branches onto the latest target IS `but pull` — never `move`, `config target`, `unapply`, or raw `git pull`/`git rebase`. The base shown in status is the last FETCHED state: when `git log` shows the remote target (for example `origin/main`) ahead of it, that is exactly the update `but pull` fetches and applies — the target setting is not stale and repointing it is never the fix. Pull carries uncommitted changes along; there is no stash, so do not hand-revert files.

### Bring in commits pushed to a branch's own remote

`but pull` only rebases onto the target. Commits someone pushed to your branch's remote show in `but status` under `(upstream: on <remote>/<branch>)`, above the branch's own commits; if status may be stale, run `but pull --check` to fetch.

1. `but branch update <branch>`, once, on the branch they pushed to.
2. Then `but pull` if the target moved too. Update before pulling. If the branch was rebased since its last push (for example by an earlier `but pull`), the update leaves an empty `(no changes)` copy of a shared commit. On a single branch, `but discard` that copy by its `#N` ref. In a stack, `but undo` the update and tell the user, because the update can also move commits into the lower branch. Do not update a second time, even if `(upstream: …)` still lists commits, because a second update duplicates commits.

### Commit selected files or hunks

1. `but diff` — shows file and hunk IDs for uncommitted changes. Do not run plain `but status` first.
2. Use file IDs when whole files belong in the commit; use hunk IDs (`<file-id>:<hunk-id>`) when only part of a file belongs. Omit IDs you don't want committed. For whole files, repo-root paths or a `dir/` prefix work too (`but commit -b feat -m "msg" src/ui/ README.md`; no `./` or globs), so don't build ID lists by piping `but diff` through grep.
3. `but commit -b <branch> -m "<msg>" <id1> <id2>` — the branch is created if it does not exist, so no prior `but branch new` is needed.
4. When the task requires knowing which changes remain, add `--status-after`; otherwise the created-commit result is sufficient.

Edge case: if wanted and unwanted edits are in the same diff hunk, GitButler cannot split that hunk by ID. Only when the task requires keeping part of that hunk uncommitted, temporarily edit the working tree to isolate the wanted lines, commit those IDs, then restore the leftover lines so they remain uncommitted.

### Amend into existing commit

1. `but status -fv` for the target commit ID and file IDs; `but diff` for hunk IDs when only part of a file belongs.
2. `but amend -t <commit-id> <id> <id>` — one command per target commit. For several target commits, chain the amends with `&&` when every target is a change-ID ref; otherwise run them one at a time with `--status-after` to get fresh refs.

### Split an existing commit

For a two-way split, move selected committed files or hunks directly into a new commit:

1. `but diff <source-commit-id>` — read committed file and hunk IDs.
2. `but split <committed-file-or-hunk-id> [<committed-file-or-hunk-id>...] -m "<message>"` — sources may mix files and hunks, but must come from one commit. The command creates the named commit immediately above the source and leaves unselected changes and the original message in the source. No follow-up reword is needed for the new commit.
3. Add `--status-after` only when the next step needs workspace IDs or details not provided by the mutation result.

For more than two replacement commits, repeat `but split ... -m "<message>"` using the remaining source's committed changes, or use the uncommit/recommit workflow below when rebuilding the entire commit:

1. `but status -fv` when you need the source commit, branch name, or placement anchor.
2. `but uncommit <source-commit-id> && but diff` in one shell call exposes the commit's changes and prints the resulting file and hunk IDs.
3. Pick replacement contents from that dirty diff, not from the old committed diff.
4. Determine the requested chronological order from the user's wording, then create the replacement commits oldest-first by chaining `but commit` calls. Do not reverse that order to match `but status`, which displays commits newest-first. `-b <branch>` puts each new commit at the TOP of that branch — if the split commit had commits above it, the replacements now sit above those preserved commits.
5. **If commits from that branch must stay ABOVE the replacements, put the preserved block back on top instead of fighting anchors.** Do not anchor with `--above <top>`/`--below <top>` (sha/`#N` anchors go stale as each insert rewrites history). Move the block together so its internal order stays intact: append `&& but move <preserved-id> [<preserved-id>...] -b <branch>` to the commit chain. Change-ID refs from step 1 stay valid; wait for fresh output first if any preserved ref is sha-based or `#N`-suffixed.
6. Leave unwanted changes uncommitted. Replacements created oldest-first appear newest-first in status — that is correct; do not reorder them. Add `--status-after` to the final mutation when you need to inspect the resulting order.

### Reorder commits

`but status` displays commits newest/top first, while task specs often list history oldest to newest — translate before moving.

1. `but status` once to get commit IDs (use `-fv` only if you also need file details).
2. `but move <source> --below <target-commit>` places source immediately below target in `but status` (older in oldest-to-newest history). `--above` places it immediately above (newer). `but move <source> -b <branch>` moves it to branch top/newest.
3. For an adjacent block, run ONE move, anchored either way: `but move <block-id> <block-id> --below <following-commit-id>` or `but move <block-id> <block-id> --above <preceding-commit-id>`. Pick an anchor outside the block; source order does not matter and the block keeps its internal order. Add `--status-after` when you need to inspect the resulting order; do not move the anchor or block members again.
4. For other reorders, make the smallest set of moves.

### Squash commits

1. `but status` for commit IDs and order.
2. Name the sources positionally and the result/target commit with `-t`: `but squash <source> [<source>...] -t <target> -m "<new message>"`.
3. To collapse an entire branch into one commit, pass just the branch and no `-t`: `but squash <branch> -m "<new message>"`.
4. Multiple independent groups may run in sequence off one status read (targets keep their change-ID refs); prefer newer/top groups first. Take fresh refs only when a ref is sha-based or `#N`-suffixed.
5. Add `--status-after` to the final squash when you need to inspect the resulting history; do not re-verify with a separate status.

### Stack existing branches

To make one existing branch depend on another: `but move <child-branch-name> --above <parent-branch-name>` (use full branch names; commit reordering uses commit IDs). To unstack: `but move <branch-name> --unstack`.

**DO NOT** stack via `uncommit` + `branch delete` + `branch new --above`, and do not use `but undo` to unstack.

### Work in a linked worktree

1. `but worktree new <branch-name>` checks out that branch in a new directory, creating it if needed (an existing branch must not be in the workspace), and prints that directory. Add `-A <branch-or-commit>` to start the branch there instead of the workspace base; it takes any Git revision, like a SHA or `origin/main`. Worktrees made by other tools must sit outside the repository directory or be listed in `.git/info/exclude`; otherwise a bare `but commit` in the main checkout records them in the branch.
2. Run `but` from that directory, or with `but -C <path>`. There, a bare `but commit -m "<msg>"` or `but diff` takes that worktree's changes, a bare path names a file there, and the commit goes on the worktree's branch. Do the work on that branch, also in a worktree another tool made. `-b <new-name>` is refused there, except in a worktree with a detached HEAD, where it names the worktree's branch; stack a new branch on it only when the user asks for a separate branch. `but undo` doesn't restore a branch a worktree has checked out. It refuses, or it reports success and leaves that branch as it is, so undoing a `move` out of the branch leaves the commit on neither branch. Reverse a command that changed the worktree's branch with its inverse (`uncommit`, `reword`, or `move` the commit back), also when you ran it from another checkout.
3. `but status` from any checkout shows the worktree as a lane of its own, with the same IDs everywhere. `@` always means the main worktree's uncommitted changes; `<worktree>:@` names a linked worktree's changes from anywhere.
4. Push and open PRs as for any branch (`but pr new <branch-name>`). `but pull` also rebases worktree branches. If that leaves a worktree commit `{conflicted}`, the branch name doesn't find it: take its commit ID from `but status` and run `but resolve conflicts <commit-id>`, then `but resolve apply <path>:<N> --commit <commit-id>`.
5. When done, `but worktree remove <name>` deletes the directory and keeps the branch. It refuses while the worktree has uncommitted changes; `-f` discards them. To delete the branch as well, run `but branch delete <name>` afterwards.

### Create or manage pull requests

`but pr new <branch-name>` pushes the selected branch and its ancestors, then creates the PR in one step — no prior `but push`. Provide `-F -` with a heredoc or `-F <file>` (first line is the title), `-t`, or `-m` with real newlines (zsh/bash: `-m $'Title\n\nBody'`) so no editor opens. Do not write the message to a file inside the repository: the next `but commit` would commit it. If forge auth is missing, ask the user to run `but config forge auth` in a terminal; it refuses non-interactive runs.

If you do create a PR for a stacked branch, use `but pr` — not `gh pr create` (only `but pr` sets PR bases and stack metadata; `gh pr create` breaks that). To publish a whole stack: `but pr new <top-branch-name> -t`. Manage with `but pr auto-merge|set-draft|set-ready <selector>`; selectors can be a branch name, current branch/stack CLI ID, or numeric review ID. See `but skill reference` for details.

When `but pr new` prints a `<pr-created>` line, copy that line into the text of your reply. It tells the app running you that this session opened the PR.

If you run in the Claude desktop app, end the `but pr new` line with the shell comment `# gh pr create`, for example `but pr new <branch-name> -F - <<'EOF' # gh pr create`. While `gitbutler/workspace` is checked out, the app counts a PR as opened by this session only when the command text contains `gh pr create`.

### Dependency conflict with another branch

Changes that build on another branch's commits cannot land on an independent branch. `but commit` and `but amend` fail atomically ("Cannot commit: N changes could not be applied"), naming the branch and commit each rejected change depends on — nothing is committed and no `-b` branch is created.

Stack only when your change builds on that branch's code. A refusal can also mean your hunk only borders lines that branch changed (a doc line, a lockfile): then leave one unchanged line between your edit and theirs, or keep that hunk uncommitted until that branch lands, and commit the rest. Never drop or rewrite real work to get past a refusal; ask the user.

When there is a single dependency branch, the error's Hint gives the exact recovery command: `but move <your-branch> --above <dependency-branch>` to stack an existing branch on its dependency, or `but branch new <name> --above <dependency-branch>` when the target branch didn't exist yet. Run it, then retry the original command. When the error names dependencies without a Hint (several dependency branches, or the dependency is on the target branch itself), run `but status -fv` to see where the dependent commits live before choosing a placement.

If that recovery command fails, do NOT try `uncommit`, `squash`, or `undo` as a workaround — re-run `but status -fv` to confirm both branches exist and are applied, then retry with exact branch names.

### Resolve conflicted commits (after pull, move, or reorder)

**NEVER use `git add`, `git commit`, `git checkout --theirs/--ours`, or any git write command during resolution.** Only `but resolve` commands plus direct file edits. The one exception is a conflicted submodule in edit mode, below.

Conflicts do not interrupt operations in GitButler: a rebase always completes, and commits that conflicted are marked `{conflicted}` in `but status`. Find them from the warning that history-editing commands (`move`, `discard`, …) print, from the `but pull` summary, or from `but status`. Resolve them one conflict at a time, without entering any mode. Resolve any uncommitted `{conflicted}` files first, as in Conflicts in uncommitted files; `apply` refuses while one is left. Work through one branch at a time, oldest commit first — the loop is:

1. `but resolve conflicts <branch>` — shows the conflicts of that branch's oldest conflicted commit, numbered per file. Each conflict has three sections: `ours` (the new base the commit was rebased onto), `base` (common ancestor), and `theirs` (the commit's own version). Without a branch it picks the first conflicted branch and tells you which; the output also says when other conflicted commits exist.
2. Apply one resolution per command:
   - Merged/mixed content (the common case — combine the intent of both sides): pipe it to `but resolve apply <path>:<N>` via stdin (heredoc) or pass `--file <f>`. The content replaces the whole conflicted region; never include conflict markers.
   - Take a side entirely: `but resolve apply <path>:<N> --ours` or `--theirs` (bare `<path>` applies the side to all conflicts in that file).
   - Delegate one conflict to the configured AI model: `but resolve apply <path>:<N> --ai` — prefer your own merged content when you have the context.
   - `apply` targets the same default commit as `conflicts`; when more than one branch is conflicted, pin it with `--commit <branch>`.
3. Go back to step 1 until it reports no conflicts. Commit ids are not stable here — every apply rewrites the commit — but branch names are, so address everything by branch and never bookkeep commit ids. Partial progress is fine: a commit with unresolved conflicts left stays `{conflicted}` with exactly those conflicts.

A wrong resolution is reverted with `but undo`.

`but resolve <commit-id> --ai` resolves a whole commit with the configured AI model in one shot, and `but resolve --ai` without a commit resolves every conflicted commit, oldest first — acceptable as a fallback, but you usually have better context than that model does, so prefer resolving the conflicts yourself with `apply`.

**Use edit mode only when you must run code against the resolution** (build/tests at that commit). Edit mode needs `gitbutler/workspace`: while a single branch is checked out, `but resolve <commit-id>` refuses, so use `apply`.

1. `but resolve <commit-id>` — enters resolution mode and prints the conflict regions.
2. **Edit the files** to remove every conflict marker — `<<<<<<<`, `|||||||` (the common-ancestor section), `=======` and `>>>>>>>` — and keep the correct content. Do NOT skip this; do NOT use `but amend` on conflicted commits.
   - A conflicted submodule has no markers and `finish` refuses until you select its side: see Conflict Resolution Mode in `but skill concepts`.
3. `but resolve finish` reports leftover markers, surviving uncommitted changes, every remaining conflicted commit, and the exact current `but resolve <id>` command. Add `--status-after` to the finish you expect to clear the last conflict only when the task needs the complete resulting workspace. When it says no conflicted commits remain, stop; do not run a verification status. Cancel instead with `but resolve cancel --force`, which drops your resolution edits; without `--force` it refuses once the conflict markers are checked out.
4. Repeat for remaining conflicted commits, oldest first — finishing a lower commit rebases the ones above it.

### Conflicts in uncommitted files

`but status` marks uncommitted files with unresolved merge conflicts `{conflicted}`; they are excluded from committable changes and outside `but resolve` mode. Edit the file to the wanted contents with no conflict markers left (or delete it), then `but resolve <path>...` to mark it resolved with that state; it then shows as an ordinary uncommitted change.

## Git-to-But Map

| git | but |
|---|---|
| `git status` | `but status` for branch/stack/commit overview; `but status -fv` for file details; `but diff` for selected dirty changes |
| `git add` + `git commit` | `but commit -b <branch> -m ... <ids>` |
| `git checkout -b` + commit | `but commit -b <new-branch> -m ... <ids>` |
| `git push` | `but push <branch-name>` |
| `git rebase -i` | `but move`, `but squash`, `but reword` |
| `git rebase --onto` | `but move <branch> --above <new-base>` |
| `git checkout -- <file>` / `git restore` | `but discard <path>`, or a hunk ID from `but diff` |
| `git cherry-pick` | `but pick` |
| `git fetch` | `but pull --check` (fetches; changes no branch) |
| `git pull` on a branch others pushed to | `but branch update <branch>`, then `but pull` |
| `git worktree add -b <branch>` | `but worktree new <branch>` |
| `git worktree remove` | `but worktree remove <name>` |
| `gh pr create` | `but pr new <branch-name> -m "Title..."` |

## Notes

- `but` needs no setup in a Git repository. `HEAD` is either one checked-out branch, marked `[HEAD]` in `but status`, or `gitbutler/workspace`, which merges every applied stack. Applying a second stack, or applying a branch while the target branch is checked out, switches to `gitbutler/workspace`; unapplying back to one stack checks that branch out again. Commands and IDs are the same either way. It does need a local branch tracking the remote's default branch: if commands fail with "No target branch is configured", run `but config target origin/main` (with the default branch's name), which creates `main` to track it if missing. Never `git branch --set-upstream-to` on your own branch, which makes that branch the target.
- `but undo` restores the whole snapshot, so uncommitted edits made after the undone operation are lost (`but redo` brings them back). Commit them first.
- Read-only git inspection (`git log`, `git blame`, `git show --stat`) is allowed.
- If `but` prints an `AGENT ACTION REQUIRED` skill warning, run the suggested command once, then reload/use the GitButler skill. If it repeats, report it instead of retrying.
- For command syntax and flags: `but skill reference`

# Skill: update-agents-md

# Update AGENTS.md

## Quick start

After completing a task that reveals a new convention, boundary, or workflow rule, append it to AGENTS.md or the appropriate sub-document. Do not let knowledge disappear with the session.

## Workflows

### 1. Post-session update

- [ ] Identify any new decisions, constraints, or patterns discovered during the session.
- [ ] Determine if the note belongs in an existing sub-document or requires a new one.
- [ ] Append the note using the same bullet style as existing entries.
- [ ] Keep entries atomic: one idea per bullet.
- [ ] If a new note contradicts an old one, update the old note in-place. AGENTS.md reflects current conventions only; do not preserve historical markers or changelog entries.

### 2. Refactor into modular sub-docs

AGENTS.md must stay short. When a section grows beyond ~50 lines, extract it:

- [ ] Create a focused sub-document under `docs/agents/` (e.g., `docs/agents/testing.md`, `docs/agents/running.md`).
- [ ] Move the detailed bullets into the sub-document.
- [ ] Replace the inline content in AGENTS.md with a link:
  `See [docs/agents/<name>.md](docs/agents/<name>.md).`
- [ ] Ensure the sub-document has a clear heading matching its topic.

### 3. Existing sub-document categories

| Topic | File |
|-------|------|
| Issue tracker | `docs/agents/issue-tracker.md` |
| Triage labels | `docs/agents/triage-labels.md` |
| Domain docs | `docs/agents/domain.md` |

Add new categories as needed under `docs/agents/`.

## Rules

- AGENTS.md is an index, not a dump. If a section exceeds 50 lines, it belongs in a sub-document.
- Use consistent bullet style (`- ` at the start of each line).
- Prefer linking over inlining. The AGENTS.md table of contents should fit on one screen.
- Update AGENTS.md **last**, after all code changes are complete, so notes reflect the final state.
- When removing obsolete notes, do not leave orphaned links in AGENTS.md. If a sub-document becomes empty, delete it and remove the link.

## Examples

### Good: Extracting an overgrown section

AGENTS.md before (52 lines under `## Testing`):

```markdown
## Testing

- Run all tests with `go test ./...` or `make test`.
- `make build` compiles all packages with `go build ./...`.
- `make build-whisper` compiles all packages including whisper.cpp CGO code...
- ... (49 more lines)
```

AGENTS.md after:

```markdown
## Testing

See [docs/agents/testing.md](docs/agents/testing.md).
```

Content moved to `docs/agents/testing.md` with the original heading preserved.

### Bad: Appending endlessly to AGENTS.md

```markdown
## Testing

- Run all tests with `go test ./...` or `make test`.
- `make build` compiles all packages with `go build ./...`.
- `make build-whisper` compiles all packages including whisper.cpp CGO code...
- ... (120 more lines)
```

This bloats the index and makes it hard to scan. Extract at ~50 lines.

## Additional prototype-only findings

All below are **throwaway, in-memory prototype workflows** under `routes/dashboard/prototype/beginners-workshop`; `bw-prototype-store.svelte.ts:1-4,1144-1171` confirms no Phoenix/API use and reset-on-reload.

### 1. In-memory Workshop lifecycle command system — **high complexity**
- **Store:** `bw-prototype-store.svelte.ts:1385-1642`
- **UI command router/forms:** `command-dialogs.svelte:11-36`, `command-dialog-body.svelte:41-161,202-740`; openers in `workshop-menu.svelte:12-55` and console variants.
- **State:** mutable `Workshop.status`, batches, cutoff, staff, finalisation/cancellation fields; `Intake.state`, person standing/carried fee, holds, emails/history.
- **Stages/transitions:**
  - `schedule` creates `scheduled` workshop (`1387-1415`).
  - `sendBatch` creates a numbered Batch plus `contacted` Intakes (`1417-1457`).
  - `reschedule` keeps workshop scheduled, truncates an open Batch window if needed, logs/emails every open Intake (`1547-1574`).
  - `cancelWorkshop`: `scheduled → cancelled`; paid Intakes → `deferred` plus held fee; contacted → `returned`; releases holds (`1576-1608`).
  - `finish`: scheduled/check-in-open → `finalised`; paid + checked-in → `attended`; paid + absent → `no_show`; updates standings and applied fees (`1610-1642`).
- **Guards:** scheduled-only, cutoff/window ordering, proposal nonempty, capacity/fee locks, no reschedule/cancel after finalisation or repeated cancellation, finish only while check-in open.
- **Why implicit:** the actual domain transition table is procedural mutations across methods, not an explicit machine. The `Phase` enum is derived from state/time (`1255-1266`) and controls command visibility in all console variants.
- **Prototype surfaces:** tabbed console `console-variant-a-tabs.svelte:137-148,333-397`; board `console-variant-b-board.svelte:231-303`; cockpit `console-variant-c-cockpit.svelte:190-244,349-377`.
- **Tests:** none found in this prototype directory.

### 2. Intake / person / carried-fee command transition system — **high complexity**
- **Store:** `bw-prototype-store.svelte.ts:1644-1826`.
- **Primary editor surface:** `intake-detail.svelte:181-307`; secondary command exposure in `console-variant-a-tabs.svelte:333-397`.
- **Transitions:**
  - `contacted → declined` and person → waiting (`decline`, `1655-1663`).
  - `paid → deferred`, creates/holds carried fee, person → waiting (`defer`, `1665-1677`).
  - `paid → cancelled_refunded`, creates successful refund; applied fee → refunded; person → waiting (`cancelWithRefund`, `1679-1694`).
  - open (`contacted|paid`) → `withdrawn` or `declined`; person → removed; optional refund/forfeit of carried fee (`withdraw`, `1696-1730`).
  - contacted + held fee → paid via carried fee, held → applied (`confirm`, `1732-1745`).
  - held/applied fee → refunded; can delegate to cancel-with-refund if it paid the open Intake (`refundCarriedFee`, `1747-1763`).
  - failed refund → succeeded by retry or manual record (`1765-1787`).
  - open Intake can resend or rotate link; rotation increments `linkGeneration` (`1789-1826`).
- **Guards:** source Intake state, held/applied fee status, payment cutoff, free seats, and failed-refund-only recovery.
- **Why implicit:** each command owns related cross-entity writes, email/history side effects, and guards; the UI branches directly on mutable fixture state.
- **Related dialog mode:** withdraw confirmation/choice at `command-dialog-body.svelte:691-739`; it branches on paid/fee state and passes the selected refund boolean into the store.
- **Tests:** none found.

### 3. Door check-in / undo / finalisation — **high**
- **Store:** check-in/undo `bw-prototype-store.svelte.ts:1828-1846`; finalisation `1610-1642`.
- **Door A:** `door-variant-a-list.svelte:14-42,118-187`.
- **Door B:** `door-variant-b-tiles.svelte:25-40,80-157`.

- **Why implicit:** persistent fixture mutations plus a local confirmation/arming protocol.

- **Store:** `bw-prototype-store.svelte.ts:1848-1882`.
- **UI:** `intake-detail.svelte:239-280`; tabbed console menu `console-variant-a-tabs.svelte:372-396`.

### 5. Invitation handoff with concurrent-refusal reconciliation — **medium-high**
- **Store:** `bw-prototype-store.svelte.ts:1884-1909`.
- **UI:** `invitable-view.svelte:12-18,51-123`; inline console action `intake-detail.svelte:255-280`; board/tabbed variants.

- **Source:** `command-dialogs.svelte:11-36`; `command-dialog-body.svelte:29-84`.

# Skill: codebase-design

# Codebase Design

Design **deep modules**: a lot of behaviour behind a small interface, placed at a clean seam, testable through that interface. Use this language and these principles wherever code is being designed or restructured. The aim is leverage for callers, locality for maintainers, and testability for everyone.

## Glossary

Use these terms exactly — don't substitute "component," "service," "API," or "boundary." Consistent language is the whole point.

**Module** — anything with an interface and an implementation. Deliberately scale-agnostic: a function, class, package, or tier-spanning slice. _Avoid_: unit, component, service.

**Interface** — everything a caller must know to use the module correctly: the type signature, but also invariants, ordering constraints, error modes, required configuration, and performance characteristics. _Avoid_: API, signature (too narrow — they refer only to the type-level surface).

**Implementation** — what's inside a module, its body of code. Distinct from **Adapter**: a thing can be a small adapter with a large implementation (a Postgres repo) or a large adapter with a small implementation (an in-memory fake). Reach for "adapter" when the seam is the topic; "implementation" otherwise.

**Depth** — leverage at the interface: the amount of behaviour a caller (or test) can exercise per unit of interface they have to learn. A module is **deep** when a large amount of behaviour sits behind a small interface, **shallow** when the interface is nearly as complex as the implementation.

**Seam** _(Michael Feathers)_ — a place where you can alter behaviour without editing in that place; the *location* at which a module's interface lives. Where to put the seam is its own design decision, distinct from what goes behind it. _Avoid_: boundary (overloaded with DDD's bounded context).

**Adapter** — a concrete thing that satisfies an interface at a seam. Describes *role* (what slot it fills), not substance (what's inside).

**Leverage** — what callers get from depth: more capability per unit of interface they learn. One implementation pays back across N call sites and M tests.

**Locality** — what maintainers get from depth: change, bugs, knowledge, and verification concentrate in one place rather than spreading across callers. Fix once, fixed everywhere.

## Deep vs shallow

**Deep module** = small interface + lots of implementation:

```
┌─────────────────────┐
│   Small Interface   │  ← Few methods, simple params
├─────────────────────┤
│                     │
│  Deep Implementation│  ← Complex logic hidden
│                     │
└─────────────────────┘
```

**Shallow module** = large interface + little implementation (avoid):

```
┌─────────────────────────────────┐
│       Large Interface           │  ← Many methods, complex params
├─────────────────────────────────┤
│  Thin Implementation            │  ← Just passes through
└─────────────────────────────────┘
```

When designing an interface, ask:

- Can I reduce the number of methods?
- Can I simplify the parameters?
- Can I hide more complexity inside?

## Principles

- **Depth is a property of the interface, not the implementation.** A deep module can be internally composed of small, mockable, swappable parts — they just aren't part of the interface. A module can have **internal seams** (private to its implementation, used by its own tests) as well as the **external seam** at its interface.
- **The deletion test.** Imagine deleting the module. If complexity vanishes, it was a pass-through. If complexity reappears across N callers, it was earning its keep.
- **The interface is the test surface.** Callers and tests cross the same seam. If you want to test *past* the interface, the module is probably the wrong shape.
- **One adapter means a hypothetical seam. Two adapters means a real one.** Don't introduce a seam unless something actually varies across it.

## Designing for testability

Good interfaces make testing natural:

1. **Accept dependencies, don't create them.**

   ```typescript
   // Testable
   function processOrder(order, paymentGateway) {}

   // Hard to test
   function processOrder(order) {
     const gateway = new StripeGateway();
   }
   ```

2. **Return results, don't produce side effects.**

   ```typescript
   // Testable
   function calculateDiscount(cart): Discount {}

   // Hard to test
   function applyDiscount(cart): void {
     cart.total -= discount;
   }
   ```

3. **Small surface area.** Fewer methods = fewer tests needed. Fewer params = simpler test setup.

## Relationships

- A **Module** has exactly one **Interface** (the surface it presents to callers and tests).
- **Depth** is a property of a **Module**, measured against its **Interface**.
- A **Seam** is where a **Module**'s **Interface** lives.
- An **Adapter** sits at a **Seam** and satisfies the **Interface**.
- **Depth** produces **Leverage** for callers and **Locality** for maintainers.

## Rejected framings

- **Depth as ratio of implementation-lines to interface-lines** (Ousterhout): rewards padding the implementation. We use depth-as-leverage instead.
- **"Interface" as the TypeScript `interface` keyword or a class's public methods**: too narrow — interface here includes every fact a caller must know.
- **"Boundary"**: overloaded with DDD's bounded context. Say **seam** or **interface**.

## Going deeper

- **Deepening a cluster given its dependencies** — see [DEEPENING.md](DEEPENING.md): dependency categories, seam discipline, and replace-don't-layer testing.
- **Exploring alternative interfaces** — see [DESIGN-IT-TWICE.md](DESIGN-IT-TWICE.md): spin up parallel sub-agents to design the interface several radically different ways, then compare on depth, locality, and seam placement.

**They can. “Doesn’t need XState” isn’t the same as “shouldn’t use XState.”** My inventory mixed substantial workflows with small interaction protocols; I should have made that distinction clearer.

Since this repo already uses XState, **standardizing custom workflows on it is reasonable**. I wouldn’t build a homemade actor runtime merely to avoid XState.

## What should—and shouldn’t—become a machine?

| Kind of state | Appropriate model |
|---|---|
| Ordered async workflow with retries, cancellation, timers, or races | **XState** |
| Small, exclusive interaction modes | XState **or** a tagged union with a pure transition function |
| Independent values, such as selected date and annual-fee preference | Machine **context**, not a state for every combination |
| Server query/cache lifecycle | Keep **TanStack Query**; add a machine only for coordination beyond fetching |
| Authoritative membership/payment/inventory lifecycle | Keep **Phoenix authoritative**; model only the browser’s interaction protocol |
| Dialog focus, keyboard navigation, editor history | Usually let **Bits UI/Tiptap/etc.** own their existing machinery |

The mistake would be creating a second machine that merely mirrors an existing owner—not using XState itself.

## How would we model a small machine without XState?

Explicitly—not by keeping the existing collection of booleans.

For example, an editor has this transition graph:

```text
closed ──OPEN──────────▶ editing
editing ──CANCEL───────▶ closed
editing ──SAVE(valid)──▶ saving
saving ──SUCCEEDED────▶ closed
saving ──FAILED───────▶ editing(error)
```

Represent its mutually exclusive states:

```ts
type EditorState =
  | { tag: "closed" }
  | { tag: "editing"; draft: Draft; error: string | null }
  | { tag: "saving"; draft: Draft };
```

Then put **every legal transition in one pure function**:

```text
transition(state, event) → { nextState, commands }
```

Entering `saving` returns a save command. Its executor performs the request and sends `SUCCEEDED` or `FAILED` back. Tests exercise that same transition function.

**The union alone isn’t the machine:** the centralized transition rules make it explicit.

That works well for something this small. Once we add delayed transitions, cancellation, stale responses, parallel work, or different retry destinations, we start rebuilding facilities XState already provides.

## My recommendation for this repo

I’d use **XState for most of the substantial workflows in the inventory**, especially:

- Notification reconnect/recovery.
- Embedded Checkout and confirmation-only retry.
- Membership reactivation.
- Announcement save sequencing.
- Inventory workbench command reconciliation.

For those, the module should expose a small interface—roughly **current state, relevant context, and `send(event)`**—and hide the sequencing inside.

I would **not** introduce separate machines for every modal wrapper, query spinner, or backend-status badge. Those generally belong inside an existing workflow, an existing library, or ordinary derived data.

So the policy could simply be:

> **Custom workflow orchestration uses XState. Existing state owners stay owners. Values are context; meaningful phases are states.**

That is more consistent—and probably better here—than maintaining two competing workflow conventions.

Replace distributed frontend workflow flags and callback sequencing with explicit XState v5 machines for the five strongest workflow families identified in the apps/web audit. This is an implementation follow-up, not another opportunity review.

Keep existing user-visible behavior, API contracts, and domain ownership. The machines own browser interaction and resource lifetimes; Phoenix remains authoritative for payment, membership, and inventory facts.

## In scope

1. **Notification connection recovery.** Model fresh-token acquisition, socket/channel lifetime, reconnect backoff, stale attempts, unauthorized termination, and teardown behind the existing connection interface.
2. **Embedded Checkout.** Convert Beginners’ Workshop Intake payment orchestration and its embedded widget lifecycle. Also convert the equivalent public regular-Workshop embedded-widget lifecycle. Preserve the distinction between retrying initialization and retrying confirmation after payment.
3. **Membership reactivation.** Model opening, saved-method lookup, selection, submission, billing-portal fallback, and reconciliation as one interaction protocol. Keep TanStack Query as the owner of server reads and cache state.
4. **Training Announcement editing.** Model create versus edit, preview, optional schedule update followed by copy update, stage-specific failure, and successful reconciliation/closure.
5. **Inventory Item workbench.** Model routed list/create/manage modes and command-result reconciliation, including draft rebasing, success feedback, deletion, and navigation. Keep independent drafts independent.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Each scoped workflow has an owning XState machine with named phases, events, guards, and lifecycle effects. Remove the procedural protocol it replaces; do not leave a second set of authoritative loading/error/success flags beside it.
- [ ] Browser actors are instance-scoped and stop with their owning workflow. Async results from an exited state, replaced route/entity, or destroyed workflow cannot mutate its replacement. Cancel underlying work where supported and safely discard late results otherwise.
- [ ] Retry resumes the appropriate stage. In particular, a failure confirming a completed payment never remounts payment collection or starts another payment attempt.
- [ ] Phoenix remains authoritative. TanStack Query remains the server-state/cache owner, and existing remote forms remain the command transport where already used. Do not duplicate their state machines merely to mirror pending flags.
- [ ] Existing refusals, warnings, privacy protections, optimistic/cache reconciliation, dirty-draft preservation, and navigation behavior remain intact. Independent controls are context or independent regions, not an exhaustive cross-product of states.
- [ ] Pure machine/actor tests cover the relevant success, refusal, stage-specific failure/retry, repeated-event, stale-result, and teardown cases with injected dependencies and deterministic time. Component tests verify the actual event wiring and rendered states. Retain existing contract-level regression coverage without duplicating superseded implementation tests.
- [ ] Relevant frontend build, typecheck, lint, focused unit/browser tests, and affected E2E scenarios are green. No backend or generated-client changes are expected.
- [ ] Update the existing workflow ownership notes where implementation changes them, especially the membership-reactivation note, without prescribing XState for unrelated UI state.

## Not in scope

Other audit candidates, prototype routes, backend lifecycle changes, new product behavior, new connection-status UI/manual reconnect controls, generic workflow frameworks, and converting every toggle, query, or form to an actor. Sources:

- apps/web/src/lib/components/notifications/NotificationCenter.svelte

Preserve the current Phoenix channel behavior rather than importing historical Supabase-session requirements from old tickets. Sources:
- apps/web/src/lib/components/beginners-workshops/intake-checkout.svelte
- apps/web/src/lib/components/beginners-workshops/intake-checkout-sdk.ts

- apps/web/src/routes/(public)/workshops/[id]/register/+page.svelte

Narrow the container/modal interaction interface rather than layering a chart over existing booleans. Preserve date/mode selection across retry, missing-method fallback, and distinct succeeded/terminal/pending/needs-action outcomes. Amount-preview failure remains non-blocking; preserve billing-date ownership and reactivation-start-window.ts. Keep the existing member/list/analytics/own-profile reconciliation.

Regression starting points: reactivate-membership-modal.browser.test.ts and apps/web/e2e/member-reactivation.spec.ts. Add controller/machine coverage for orchestration and stale results.

Source: apps/web/src/lib/components/training-announcements/AnnouncementSheet.svelte, with cache interactions in AnnouncementsRail.svelte and lib/training-announcements/.

Preserve optimistic creation/replacement/rollback and authoritative reconciliation. Existing edits conditionally save schedule before copy; a schedule refusal must never trigger copy update. Cover copy failure after a successful schedule write without pretending the two requests are atomic or automatically rolled back. Preserve warnings and field problems, and distinguish this workflow from the backend Discord delivery lifecycle.

Regression starting points: AnnouncementsRail.browser.test.ts and the existing announcement/copy helper tests. Add focused machine and editor-wiring tests for both save stages.

Sources:
- apps/web/src/routes/dashboard/inventory/items/[[itemId]]/item-workbench.svelte.ts
- apps/web/src/routes/dashboard/inventory/items/[[itemId]]/data.remote.ts
- apps/web/src/lib/inventory/property-values.ts

Keep createCursorTableUrl, inventoryCommand, the Valibot/remote-form field bindings, and the one remote-form path for every Item command. Model workflow modes and command progression, not independent property values as chart states. Preserve rebasedDrafts: a successful command resets its own draft while retaining unrelated unsaved changes unless their authoritative backing facts changed. Preserve cache adoption, success-flash timing, deep links, and create/delete navigation. Route changes and teardown must not leave delayed navigation or stale reconciliation targeting another Item.

Regression starting points: item-workbench.svelte.browser.test.ts, property-values.test.ts, and the affected inventory E2E scenarios.

### Verification

Use apps/web workspace scripts for build, check, and lint, plus focused Vitest unit/browser runs and affected Playwright scenarios. Update tests at the owning module interface; keep a small rendering/wiring suite. Do not run Phoenix codegen or change API contracts as part of this frontend-only refactor.

+++`

const r1 = `## Problem Statement

A member with the dashboard open stops receiving live notification signals after their laptop sleeps, the network blips, or a short-lived socket token expires. Recovery from a dead socket — fetching a fresh token, backing off, retiring the old socket, rejoining the channel — is encoded as scattered flags and callbacks inside the notification realtime bridge. Every recovery edge case (a token resolving late, a retired socket reviving itself, a hanging token fetch) must be threaded through that procedural code by hand, and each one risks either a second reconnect loop competing with Phoenix's own channel machinery or a leak that keeps fetching tokens for a page the member already left.

## Solution

Express the connection's lifecycle as one explicit XState machine behind the existing connection interface: fresh-token acquisition, socket and channel lifetime, reconnect backoff, stale-attempt handling, unauthorized termination, and teardown become named phases with guards. The notification center keeps calling the same connection factory and receiving the same handle; inside, every recovery rule is visible and testable, and stopping the machine is the entire cleanup story.

## User Stories

1. As a member with the dashboard open, I want new notifications to appear without reloading, so that I see club messages as they happen.
2. As a member whose laptop slept, I want the bridge to reconnect automatically with a fresh socket token, so that live updates resume without a reload.
3. As a member on a flaky connection, I want reconnect attempts to back off up to a ceiling, so that a failing token endpoint is not hammered.
4. As a member whose connection recovers, I want the backoff reset after a successful rejoin, so that the next blip retries quickly.
5. As a member, I want events missed while disconnected recovered by an authoritative refetch on every successful join or rejoin, so that I never silently miss a notification.
6. As a member whose session has expired, I want recovery to stop cleanly, so that the browser does not endlessly request socket tokens it can no longer obtain.
7. As a member, I want HTTP queries and mutations to keep working regardless of realtime state, so that a dead socket never breaks the rest of the dashboard.
8. As a member navigating away, I want the channel left, the socket disconnected, and all scheduled work cancelled, so that no tokens are fetched for a page I have left.
9. As a member, I want a token fetch that hangs abandoned after a timeout and retried, so that a slow endpoint cannot wedge reconnection forever.
10. As a member, I want a token that resolves after teardown or after a newer attempt dropped, so that a stale credential cannot hijack the connection.
11. As a member, I want a retired socket that revives itself disconnected again, so that two sockets never compete for one channel.
12. As a member whose channel drops while the socket stays connected, I want Phoenix's own channel rejoin to handle it, so that two reconnect loops never race.
13. As a developer, I want the connection lifecycle as named machine phases, so that adding a recovery rule means adding a transition rather than threading another flag.
14. As a developer, I want the running actor scoped to the connection handle, so that a stopped actor cannot mutate a replacement connection.
15. As a developer, I want the socket, token fetcher, and invalidation injected, so that the machine is testable without the real Phoenix client.
16. As a developer, I want the existing public connection interface preserved, so that the notification center component needs no changes.
17. As a developer, I want deterministic machine tests for success, unauthorized termination, stale results, repeated events, and teardown, so that recovery regressions are caught before review.

## Implementation Decisions

- One XState v5 machine owns the bridge recovery lifecycle: fresh-token acquisition, socket construction, channel join, error/close-driven retirement, bounded backoff, unauthorized termination, and teardown.
- The existing connection factory interface and handle are preserved; the notification center component is unchanged.
- Socket construction, socket-token fetching, and invalidation stay injected dependencies, with the real Phoenix socket factory as the default.
- Phoenix's own channel rejoin on a still-connected socket stays as-is; the machine must not add a second reconnect loop that competes with it, and socket construction keeps the neutralized reconnect delay.
- The current backoff schedule and ceiling, token-fetch timeout, reset-on-successful-join, and invalidation on every successful join/rejoin and creation signal are preserved exactly.
- An unauthorized session is a terminal event: the machine stops rather than retrying. Everything else remains best-effort with diagnostic warnings and never throws to the caller.
- Stale-attempt rules become guards and events: a token resolved after teardown or after a newer attempt is discarded; a socket or widget resolved after disposal is destroyed; a retired socket's revival is disconnected again.
- The channel keeps carrying only the best-effort creation signal; notification data, pagination, and unread counts stay owned by the Phoenix HTTP API — the machine never caches notification content.
- Machine definitions may be module-scoped; the running actor's lifetime is the returned handle. No snapshot persistence, and no shared module-level actor.

## Testing Decisions

- A good test asserts observable behavior at the connection seam: given injected socket, token, and invalidation doubles, what the handle does (connects, disconnects, leaves, invalidates, fetches tokens, stops) — never internal flag names.
- Pure machine tests with fake timers cover: first connect; token failure, empty result, and hang; unauthorized termination; socket error and close; backoff progression and reset; stale token and late socket; retired-socket revival; repeated events; idempotent destroy.
- The existing handle-level bridge test suite stays as the regression net, adapted to the same observable effects.
- Prior art: the existing notification realtime bridge tests with their injected socket and token doubles, and the pure transition tests of the invitation-acceptance decision machine.

## Out of Scope

New connection-status UI or manual reconnect controls; changes to Phoenix's channel protocol or the socket-token endpoint; importing historical Supabase-session requirements from old tickets; caching notification data in machine context; converting the Web Push subscription workflow, which is already a centralized workflow by design.

## Further Notes

Implements candidate 1 of ALE-446. The old Supabase-era notification recovery ticket (ALE-143) stays superseded; do not import its requirements. The machine owns the browser connection only — the notification row, its keyed seam, and the Web Push fan-out remain untouched.`;

const r2 = `## Problem Statement

A person paying for a Beginners' Workshop place, or a member registering for a regular Workshop, goes through an embedded Stripe Checkout widget whose lifecycle — initialize, mount, complete, confirm with Phoenix, retry, dispose — is spread across component flags and callbacks in two separate implementations: the Intake checkout widget with the Intake page's payment orchestration, and the regular-Workshop registration page. The critical safety rule — a failure confirming an already-completed payment must retry only confirmation and must never remount payment collection or start another payment attempt — exists only as carefully ordered procedural code. The regular-Workshop variant has no direct lifecycle test coverage at all.

## Solution

Each domain gets a component-scoped XState machine owning its embedded-widget lifecycle: initialization, mounted widget, confirmation, distinct failure targets with distinct retry targets, and disposal. The Intake orchestration (automatic one-shot payment start, session resume, pending-payment refresh, the Carried Fee confirm alternative) and the regular-Workshop registration flow keep their existing behavior and domain protocols, with retry-after-completion structurally impossible to misroute.

## User Stories

1. As a person opening an Intake email link, I want payment to open automatically, so that I can pay without hunting for a button.
2. As a person, I want the page's plain read to never reserve a place, so that previewing the email link does not take a Seat Hold.
3. As a person with a live hold, I want the same Checkout session resumed, so that I am never charged twice for one place.
4. As a person paying, I want the embedded widget to appear promptly with a loading indication, so that I know payment is starting.
5. As a person whose widget fails to initialize, I want a retry that starts initialization over, so that a transient Stripe failure does not dead-end my place.
6. As a person who completed payment in the widget, I want Phoenix to decide the outcome, so that the browser never claims a success Stripe did not confirm.
7. As a person whose confirmation request fails after paying, I want to retry only the confirmation, so that I am never asked to pay a second time.
8. As a person, I want the payment-in-progress refresh to reload Phoenix's view, so that a payment completed elsewhere is reflected on my page.
9. As a person holding a workshop credit (Carried Fee), I want "Confirm my place" instead of Pay, so that my prepaid place is used rather than recharged.
10. As a person, I want fixed safe error copy when Stripe fails, so that error details that may contain credentials are never shown to me.
11. As a person navigating away mid-payment, I want the widget destroyed and late SDK results discarded, so that nothing leaks or fires into a dead page.
12. As a member registering for a regular Workshop, I want the same embedded lifecycle — initialization, mounted, failure, completion — so that registration is as reliable as Intake payment.
13. As a member whose regular-Workshop checkout fails to initialize, I want a retry that restarts initialization, so that I can recover without reloading the page.
14. As a developer, I want the retry distinction (initialization versus confirmation) encoded as distinct machine states, so that remounting payment collection after completion is unrepresentable.
15. As a developer, I want Stripe SDK resources behind the injected adapter, so that the machines are testable without Stripe.
16. As a developer, I want component-scoped actors that stop with the widget, so that a destroyed checkout cannot mutate its replacement.
17. As a developer, I want direct lifecycle coverage for the regular-Workshop widget, so that its conversion is not verified only end-to-end.
18. As a developer, I want the two domain protocols kept separate, so that Seat Hold semantics and regular Workshop registration never merge into a generic checkout framework.

## Implementation Decisions

- Two machines — Beginners' Intake payment and regular-Workshop registration — sharing a shape, not a generic framework: their domain protocols stay distinct.
- The Intake machine covers: the mounted automatic payment start (once per instance, as a browser POST only), session resume, widget mount, the Stripe completion callback, Phoenix confirmation, the pending-payment refresh, the Carried Fee confirm alternative, initialization-failure retry, confirmation-only retry, and teardown.
- Confirmation is a separate phase from payment collection: entering it destroys the widget, and its failure state offers only confirmation retry — payment collection cannot remount from there.
- The automatic start stays a mounted-browser POST; a plain read or prefetch never acquires a Seat Hold; Phoenix resumes the existing session rather than creating again, and the client secret is never persisted.
- The one-shot initiation guard, the pending-payment refresh cadence, refusal rendering, and the Intake link privacy rules (token redaction, no referrer) are preserved. Client secrets and raw SDK errors are never logged.
- The regular-Workshop machine covers the same embedded lifecycle for the registration flow, preserving its flow-error surface and current user-visible behavior.
- Stripe stays behind the existing injected adapter; widgets or sessions that resolve after disposal are destroyed immediately; a stopped actor discards late callbacks.
- Actors are created per component through the Svelte integration; definitions are module-scoped; no snapshot persistence.

## Testing Decisions

- Test at the widget-component seam (client secret and confirm callback in; loading, active, failed, and completed phases out) and the Intake page seam (safe view and one-shot POST in; refresh and refusal behavior out), using a fake Stripe adapter.
- Pure machine tests cover: successful payment; initialization failure then initialization retry; completion callback into confirmation; confirmation failure then confirmation-only retry (asserting collection never remounts and no second payment attempt starts); disposal mid-initialization and mid-confirmation; repeated events; late-resolved SDK instances.
- New component-level lifecycle coverage for the regular-Workshop embedded widget — the one confirmed new seam.
- The existing Intake checkout browser tests, the Intake page browser and unit tests, and the affected end-to-end scenarios stay as regression nets.
- Prior art: the workshop express-checkout machine and its tests (stage-aware retry, no new PaymentIntent on completion failure), and the invitation-acceptance payment machine.

## Out of Scope

Hosted-checkout migration; changes to Seat Hold, Payment Window, or refund semantics (all Phoenix-owned); merging the two domains into one framework; the workshop express-checkout machine (already explicit); pre-migration hosted-mode replays; new payment or Intake copy.

## Further Notes

Implements candidate 2 of ALE-446. Phoenix stays authoritative for payment outcomes; the Stripe webhook subscription requirements are unchanged.`;

const r3 = `## Problem Statement

An operator reactivating a lapsed member goes through a dialog that lazily fetches the saved SEPA method preview, keys an amounts query off the operator's start-date and annual-fee-mode selection, submits the reactivation, and reconciles the membership queries — with the flow's phases (open, method lookup, selection, submission, billing-portal fallback, outcomes) coordinated across two components' flags and callbacks. Which outcome the operator sees — succeeded, terminal, pending, or needs-action — and what survives a retry are consequences of code ordering rather than an explicit protocol, and late async results can in principle land in a dialog that has since been reopened for a different member.

## Solution

The reactivation interaction becomes one explicit XState machine behind a narrowed modal interface: the machine owns opening, saved-method lookup, selection, submission, the billing-portal fallback, and outcome reporting, while TanStack Query remains the owner of every server read and all cache state. The operator sees exactly the dialog behavior they see today; the protocol that produces it becomes named, guarded, and deterministically testable.

## User Stories

1. As an operator, I want to open a reactivation dialog for a lapsed member, so that I can bring them back into membership.
2. As an operator, I want the saved SEPA method fetched while the dialog is open, so that I know what will be charged before charging.
3. As an operator, I want to choose a start date and an annual fee mode, so that the charge matches what the member agreed.
4. As an operator, I want the amounts recomputed for my selection, so that the preview never misstates what will be charged.
5. As an operator, I want an amount-preview failure to degrade gracefully, so that a failed preview never blocks a valid charge.
6. As an operator, I want my date and fee-mode selection preserved across a failed submission and retry, so that I do not re-enter the agreement.
7. As an operator reactivating a member with no saved method, I want the billing-portal fallback, so that payment can still be arranged.
8. As an operator, I want distinct outcomes reported — succeeded, terminal, pending, needs-action — so that I know whether to tell the member it is done or to check their bank app.
9. As an operator, I want submission errors surfaced inside the modal, so that I can retry without losing context.
10. As an operator, I want a successful reactivation to reconcile the member's profile, the member list, members analytics, and my own profile where relevant, so that the dashboard reflects it immediately.
11. As an operator closing and reopening the dialog for a different member, I want the previous member's late async results discarded, so that one member's preview can never leak into another member's dialog.
12. As an operator, I want billing dates shown exactly as Phoenix computes them, so that the monthly and annual anchors are never locally derived.
13. As a member being reactivated, I want the start-date window to follow Phoenix's UTC window, so that I am never offered an invalid start date.
14. As a developer, I want the interaction protocol as one machine, so that open, lookup, selection, submission, and outcomes are visible transitions.
15. As a developer, I want TanStack Query still owning reads and cache, so that the machine never becomes a second fetch layer.
16. As a developer, I want a narrowed modal interface rather than a chart layered over the existing booleans, so that the presentational components stay thin.
17. As a developer, I want machine tests for orchestration and stale results, so that cross-member leaks are caught deterministically.

## Implementation Decisions

- One machine owns the interaction: open, saved-method lookup, selection, amount-preview wiring, submission, billing-portal fallback, outcome reporting, and close/reopen.
- The dialog/modal interface is narrowed (member context in; preview state, selection, submission, and outcomes out) rather than layering a machine over existing booleans; the presentational modal keeps the date picker, radio group, and copy.
- TanStack Query remains the server-state owner: the preview, amounts, billing-portal, and reactivation requests stay generated query and mutation options; the machine sends events and reacts to their results, never fetching or caching itself.
- The selection (start date, annual fee mode) lives in machine context and is preserved across submission failure and retry.
- Amount-preview failure stays non-blocking: the modal hides amounts and keeps the form usable; a missing saved method switches to the billing-portal fallback path.
- The outcome vocabulary is unchanged — succeeded, terminal, pending, needs-action — still reported as toasts, now driven by machine states.
- Reconciliation on success is unchanged: the member profile, member list, members analytics, own profile, and the caller-side settle hook.
- Billing-date ownership stays with Phoenix's billing anchors: the frontend only formats the returned civil dates, and the start-date window continues to follow Phoenix's UTC window through the existing reactivation start-window module.
- A per-dialog actor is created on open and stopped on close; late results from a previous member's dialog are discarded by the stopped actor; no snapshot persistence.

## Testing Decisions

- Test at the modal/dialog seam: member context and injected query/mutation doubles in; observable selection, fallback, outcome, and reconciliation effects out.
- Pure machine tests cover: open through lookup, selection, and submission to succeeded; no saved method switching to the portal fallback; submission failure then retry with the selection preserved; pending, needs-action, and terminal outcomes; closing mid-flight; reopening for a different member discarding stale results; repeated events.
- The existing reactivation modal browser test and the member-reactivation end-to-end scenario stay as regression nets, adapted to the narrowed interface.
- Prior art: the reactivation modal browser tests, the member-reactivation end-to-end scenario, and the invitation-acceptance payment machine tests for outcome and stale-result patterns.

## Out of Scope

New reactivation product behavior or pricing rules; backend changes to the preview, amounts, or reactivation contracts; moving reactivation off TanStack Query; converting the member list or profile pages; XState for unrelated member dialogs.

## Further Notes

Implements candidate 3 of ALE-446. The standing note that membership reactivation stays on TanStack Query remains true — the machine owns the interaction, not server state — so update that note's wording only if implementation changes what it says.`;

const r4 = `## Problem Statement

A trainer saving a training announcement goes through a carefully ordered sequence — create, or conditionally update the schedule before the copy — coordinated by procedural async code in the announcement editor sheet. The ordering rules exist for safety: an elapsed slot is refused before any copy is written, a schedule refusal must never trigger a copy write, and a copy-only edit carries no warnings. But they are enforced only by code order, and a copy failure after a successful schedule write leaves the editor in a state whose meaning depends on which flags happened to be set. Preview, field problems, and warnings each add more flags on top.

## Solution

The save workflow becomes an explicit XState machine: create versus edit paths, the optional schedule stage followed by the copy stage, stage-specific failure with stage-specific retry targets, and successful reconciliation and closure. The two edit requests stay non-atomic by design — the machine makes that visible instead of papering over it — and every stage's failure lands in a named state.

## User Stories

1. As a trainer, I want to create a new training announcement with its schedule and copy in one save, so that I do not need two passes.
2. As a trainer, I want an elapsed-slot schedule edit refused before any copy is written, so that a rejected edit never half-applies.
3. As a trainer editing only the copy, I want no schedule warnings surfaced, so that the save result reflects only what I changed.
4. As a trainer editing both, I want the schedule saved first and then the copy, so that the refusal ordering above always holds.
5. As a trainer, I want a schedule-stage failure to leave the copy unwritten, so that I can fix the schedule and save again.
6. As a trainer whose copy write fails after a successful schedule write, I want a clear stage-specific failure, so that I know the schedule edit landed and the copy did not.
7. As a trainer, I want that partial state reported honestly with no pretend rollback, so that I re-save knowing what already applied.
8. As a trainer, I want field problems and warnings rendered per stage, so that I know exactly what to fix.
9. As a trainer, I want a live preview while editing, so that I can check the copy before saving.
10. As a trainer, I want optimistic creation and replacement with rollback on failure, so that the rail reflects my save immediately but never lies.
11. As a trainer, I want a successful save reconciled with authoritative server state and the sheet closed, so that the list shows the saved announcement.
12. As a trainer closing the sheet mid-save, I want late results discarded, so that a closed editor cannot mutate the rail underneath me.
13. As a developer, I want create and edit as distinct machine paths, so that their different stage sequences are visible.
14. As a developer, I want stage-specific failure states with correct retry targets, so that a retry never blindly re-runs a completed stage.
15. As a developer, I want the mutations injected, so that the machine is testable without the API client.
16. As a developer, I want machine tests for both save stages, so that the ordering rules are asserted rather than assumed.

## Implementation Decisions

- One machine owns the save workflow: the create path (a single create request), the edit path (an optional schedule stage gated on an actual schedule change, then the copy stage), stage-specific failure, success reconciliation and closure.
- The two edit requests stay separate and non-atomic by design; there is no invented rollback of a successful schedule write — the copy-failure state surfaces what already applied.
- The schedule stage runs only when the schedule actually changed; its warnings flow to the finished result; a copy-only edit carries none.

const r5 = `## Problem Statement

The quartermaster Items page is a routed workflow — list, create, and manage modes with URL-backed selection, one remote form per Item command, and draft rebasing across the page's forms — coordinated by the extracted runes controller. 2. As an operator, I want search and filter changes to reset paging while paging pushes history, so that the URL always matches the view.
3. As an operator deep-linking an item code or slug, I want it resolved to the item's route, so that shared links land on the right item.
4. As an operator opening the create route, I want the create form, so that I can add an item.

6. As an operator, I want a successful command to adopt the item Phoenix answered with, so that the page never trusts a locally edited copy.
7. As an operator, I want only the submitting form's drafts reset on success, so that my unsaved edits in other forms survive.
8. As an operator, I want an unrelated unsaved edit rebased only if Phoenix's answer changed what that form edits, so that I neither lose work needlessly nor keep stale work.
9. As an operator, I want a per-command toast and a success flash on the submit button, so that I can see which action landed.
10. As an operator, I want creation to navigate to the new item and deletion to return to the list, so that the route always follows the workflow.
11. As an operator, I want the right caches refreshed per command, so that lists, maintenance views, and structure stay authoritative.
12. As an operator navigating mid-command, I want no delayed navigation or stale reconciliation aimed at the previous item, so that the page never jumps after I have left.
13. As an operator, I want property values edited independently, so that filling one property does not disturb another.
14. As a developer, I want routed modes as machine states, so that mode transitions (select, create, delete navigation) are visible and exhaustive.
15. As a developer, I want command progression as machine events with per-command outcomes, so that each command's refresh, rebase, and navigation effects are declared once.
